summaries.example: Maya practices drawing because her classmate Leo is very good at it. She feels sad that she cannot draw as well. If Maya wants to improve her own drawing, that may be an emulative desire. If what especially bothers her is that Leo has the skill, her feeling may be closer to envy. The difference matters because envy is about comparison with another person, not just wanting something.
summaries.summary: Envy is a complicated emotion about comparison. An envier feels distress because another person has a good, skill, or advantage that the envier lacks. The “good” might be an object, a talent, happiness, or another valuable condition. Many philosophers think envy also includes wanting the other person not to have the good, but others disagree. They ask whether a person can feel a milder, helpful kind of envy while simply trying to improve. Envy is different from jealousy, which mainly concerns losing someone’s affection, and from resentment, which includes a complaint about unfairness. Philosophers also ask whether envy is always harmful or irrational. Usually it feels bad and may hurt self-respect, but its assessment can depend on whether the comparison is accurate and whether the difference really harms the person who feels envy.
key_ideas: Envy is more than a simple feeling. It can include thoughts, feelings, wishes, and body reactions.
Envy usually involves a person who compares themself with another person who has some good, skill, or advantage.
Philosophers disagree about whether envy must include wanting the other person to lose the advantage.
Envy, jealousy, and resentment are related but different emotions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding envy can help us notice the difference between wanting to grow and wanting another person to lose what they have. It also helps us think carefully about fairness. A person may dislike an unequal situation because it seems unfair, or because they feel envy; those are not automatically the same reason.

important_terms.definition: A strong, unpleasant feeling that someone else has something good that you do not have, especially when you compare yourself with that person.
A feeling focused on losing someone’s affection to a rival. Jealousy and envy can look similar, but they have different main concerns.
A feeling or wish connected to fairness, right, or wrong. Resentment usually includes a complaint that someone has been treated wrongly.
Wanting to have a skill or good that another person has, without wanting that person to lose it.

questions_to_think_about: Can you want something another person has without envying that person?
How is being jealous of a friend’s attention different from envying a classmate’s skill?
Could feeling envious ever encourage someone to work harder?
Why might it be important to tell envy apart from a complaint about unfairness?

summaries.example: Suppose Alex and Jordan are equally interested in a competitive scholarship. Jordan receives it, and Alex feels distressed. If Alex is upset because the selection was unfair, the emotion may be resentment. If Alex is upset because Jordan has the scholarship and Alex does not, especially as a competitive comparison, it may be envy. Alex might still refuse to sabotage Jordan. This does not by itself settle whether Alex lacks any wish that Jordan lose the advantage: philosophers disagree about whether such a wish is part of envy even when the person would never act on it.
summaries.summary: The entry treats envy as an emotional syndrome: a partly connected pattern of thoughts, feelings, motivations, and bodily responses. Its central structure involves a subject, a rival, and a good that the subject takes the rival to possess. Envy is usually understood as distress at an unfavorable comparison, together with a desire for the good. A major dispute concerns whether genuine envy also requires a desire that the rival lose the good. Defenders of benign or emulative envy describe cases in which a person is pained by inferiority but seeks only self-improvement. Critics argue that such cases may be longing or emulative desire rather than envy, which they regard as essentially competitive. The entry also distinguishes envy from jealousy and resentment. Jealousy focuses on a beloved’s affection; resentment includes a moral complaint. These distinctions shape debates about rationality. Envy may be imprudent because it damages well-being or self-respect, yet its fittingness depends on whether the rival has the good, whether the good is genuinely valuable, and whether the comparison is bad for the subject. Political debates ask whether equality is sought from envy or from concerns about justice, and distinguish the emotion from the technical idea of an envy-free distribution.
key_ideas: A standard analysis of envy includes distress over an unfavorable comparison and a desire for the good possessed by the rival; whether it also requires a desire to deprive the rival is disputed.
The distinction between benign and invidious envy may reflect either two forms of one emotion or a confusion between envy and emulative desire.
Jealousy is primarily concerned with a beloved’s affection, while envy is primarily concerned with the rival and the rival’s advantage.
Resentment is normally a moral emotion because it includes a complaint about wrong or injustice; envy need not include such a complaint.
Judging envy involves different questions: whether it is good for the person to have, whether its appraisal is accurate, and whether it is morally acceptable.
The charge that egalitarian views are motivated by envy is controversial, since concern about unequal advantages may instead express resentment about injustice.
summaries.why_it_matters: The analysis shows why judging an emotion requires more than calling it good or bad. We must identify what the emotion represents, what motivates it, and whether that appraisal is accurate. The distinctions also prevent a moral complaint about unfairness from being dismissed as mere envy. In political philosophy, this matters when assessing arguments about equality, distribution, and the effects of large differences in social standing.

important_terms.definition: An emotion involving an envier, a rival, and a good, capacity, or trait that the envier believes the rival has and the envier lacks.
The philosophical idea that an emotion’s appraisal fits reality: for example, envy would be unfitting if the rival did not really have the supposed good.
The idea that an emotion is supported by what the subject has reason to believe, even if the belief later turns out to be mistaken.
A proposed form of envy in which the subject seeks to improve their own position without wanting the rival brought down. Some philosophers deny that this is envy proper.
A moral emotion involving a complaint that someone or something is wrong or unjust. Philosophers commonly distinguish it from envy, though both may occur together.
An emotion centered on a beloved person’s affection and the fear of losing it to a rival. Envy instead centers more directly on the rival’s possession of a good.
A preference for a situation in which neither the subject nor the rival has a good over one in which only the rival has it. Philosophers use this idea to analyze envy’s possible irrationality.
A distribution of resources in which no person prefers another person’s bundle to their own. Here “envy” is a technical label, not necessarily the emotion discussed in the entry.

questions_to_think_about: If someone wants a rival’s advantage removed but would never act to remove it, is that desire still part of the emotion?
Is a painful wish for another person’s skill simply longing, or can it be envy? What psychological evidence would distinguish them?
Can an unfavorable comparison be bad for a person even when the person’s own possessions have not changed?
Why does the distinction between envy and resentment matter when evaluating egalitarian political views?
Should the fact that an emotion is harmful to its subject be enough to show that it is irrational or morally wrong?

summaries.example: Nora and Sam both try out for the school play. Sam gets the lead, and Nora feels bad. If Nora thinks the director treated her unfairly, her feeling may be resentment. If she mainly hates that Sam has the role while she does not, it may be envy. If Nora studies acting and hopes to earn a lead next time without wishing Sam to fail, some philosophers would call this benign envy. Others would call it admiration, longing, or emulative desire instead.
summaries.summary: Envy is an emotion involving a person who compares themself with a rival who is believed to possess some good, such as a possession, ability, status, happiness, or other valued condition. The envier is distressed by lacking it and typically wants it. Philosophers disagree about whether envy also includes wanting the rival to lose the good. This produces a debate about “benign” or emulative envy. On one view, someone can be pained by inferiority while trying only to improve their own position. On another, envy is essentially competitive: its dissatisfaction is directed toward overcoming or undoing the rival’s advantage, even if other values stop the person from acting on that impulse. Envy differs from jealousy because jealousy centers on a beloved’s affection, while envy centers on the rival’s advantage. It differs from resentment because resentment involves a moral complaint about unfairness. The entry also asks whether envy is rational. It may be harmful to the person who feels it, but its fittingness depends on facts about the rival, the good, and whether the difference itself is bad for the subject. These distinctions are important in arguments about equality and justice.
key_ideas: Philosophers generally treat envy and jealousy as different emotions, even though everyday speech often mixes the words.
The main disagreement about benign envy is not just about vocabulary; it concerns how human emotions should be classified and explained.
Envy is usually considered harmful or imprudent, but whether it is irrational depends partly on whether the comparison really makes the subject worse off.
Resentment and envy can occur together, but resentment includes a judgment about injustice while envy does not necessarily do so.
A criticism of egalitarianism based on envy is difficult to establish because opposition to inequality may express concern for justice instead.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often use “envy” as a quick explanation for disagreement about unequal outcomes. Philosophy asks whether that explanation is justified. Careful distinctions can show when someone is competing, when someone is trying to improve, and when someone is objecting to injustice. They also help explain why an emotion may be understandable without automatically being wise, accurate, or morally acceptable.

important_terms.definition: An unpleasant emotion in which a person is distressed by another person’s possession of a good, ability, or advantage that the person lacks.
An emotion mainly concerned with a loved person’s attention or affection being threatened by a rival.
A moral emotion that involves judging or complaining that someone has acted wrongly or that a situation is unjust.
A proposed kind of envy in which someone wants to improve their own position but does not want the rival to lose the advantage.
Wanting a good or ability because another person has it, while not wanting that person to lose it. Some philosophers say this is not envy proper.
Whether an emotion’s view of a situation matches the facts. Envy may be unfitting if the rival lacks the supposed good or the supposed good is not really valuable.
A way of distributing resources so that no one prefers another person’s share to their own. This uses “envy” in a technical sense.

questions_to_think_about: What separates envy from simply wanting to learn or obtain what another person has?
Could a person feel genuine envy while sincerely refusing to harm the rival?
If a rival gained an advantage through cheating, would envy directed at that advantage seem more fitting? Why?
Why might people be most envious of those they see as competitors rather than of people far above them?
What is the difference between an emotional motive for equality and a principle that unequal treatment is unjust?
